diagnosis.message: Hello! Today we learn SQL joins. If student names are in one register and book loans in another, how would you find which student has which book?

explain.message: Think of two registers in a college library. One lists students with their roll numbers. The other lists loans: roll number, book and due date. To answer who has which book, you match the roll numbers across both registers. That is a JOIN. ON says which columns must match, usually a foreign key like student_id to the student's id. INNER JOIN keeps only matches. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even with no match, filling the rest with NULL. Shall we find overdue books?
explain.code:
SELECT s.name, b.title, l.due_date
FROM loans l
JOIN students s ON s.id = l.student_id
JOIN books b    ON b.id = l.book_id
WHERE l.returned = false;

-- every student, even with no loans
SELECT s.name, COUNT(l.id) FROM students s
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.name;
explain.mermaid:
erDiagram
  STUDENTS ||--o{ LOANS : borrows
  BOOKS ||--o{ LOANS : "is lent in"

example.message: From loans, JOIN students ON students.id equals loans.student_id, and JOIN books ON books.id equals loans.book_id. WHERE returned is false gives every unreturned book with the student's name. To list every student, even those with no loans, use students LEFT JOIN loans and count. Why would an INNER JOIN miss some students here?
example.code:
SELECT s.name, b.title, l.due_date
FROM loans l
JOIN students s ON s.id = l.student_id
JOIN books b    ON b.id = l.book_id
WHERE l.returned = false;

-- every student, even with no loans
SELECT s.name, COUNT(l.id) FROM students s
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.name;

another_way.message: Another way: a wedding seating list. One list has guest names and table numbers, another has table numbers and the food served. Matching on table number tells you what each guest eats. Guests without a table would drop out with an INNER JOIN. Which join keeps them?

doubt.answer: Good doubt. Without ON, or with a wrong condition, every row joins with every row, giving a huge result. Always match on a key. Does that help?

code.prompt: Show each unreturned loan with the student's name, joining loans and students on the student id.

questions: In a {context}, data is in two tables linked by an id. Explain how you would join them to answer a question, and what ON does.
Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN with an example from a {context}.
A join on a {context} returns far too many rows. Explain the likely mistake and how to fix it.

feedback.good: You matched the tables on the right key.
feedback.missing: Explain which rows each join type keeps, especially LEFT JOIN.
